refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: systemd-device-accept-d.service is a system service that applies the device acceptance configuration to devices, i.e. it writes the requested trust policy configured for a device in accept.d5 to the trust_policy attribute in the sysfs directory of the device. The separate read-only trust attribute reports the active level resolved by the kernel for the current binding, or disabled when no driver is bound.

The kernel only allows changing the requested policy before the first matching or probing attempt that locks it. A failed or deferred probe and unbinding the driver do not make it writable again. Hence the service is part of sysinit.target, and thus also runs in the initrd, once sysfs is available with the devices the kernel has registered so far. When it is started, it applies the configuration to the devices that exist already, and only then reports that start-up is complete. It is ordered before systemd-udevd.service, which loads the kernel modules for devices, and before any other service that loads kernel modules. After that, the service keeps running and listens to the uevents of the kernel, and applies the configuration to devices as they are added, for example by hotplug. Only add uevents are considered.

The service is only started if one of the accept.d/ directories is not empty. Failing to apply the trust level to a device is logged, and the service carries on. When the system switches from the initrd to the root file system, the service is stopped, and started again with the configuration of the root file system. To have devices configured in the initrd, the configuration files and the service have to be included in the initrd.

Note that the trust level cannot be changed for devices that have been probed already, for example because their drivers are built into the kernel, or because they were added before the service was started. When a device is added while its driver is loaded, the kernel probes it right away. When the driver is a kernel module that is not loaded yet, the service handles the uevent of the device in parallel to systemd-udevd.service, which loads the module. The service gets the uevent directly from the kernel and only writes a sysfs attribute, which is usually done long before udev has processed the uevent, but this is not guaranteed. The trust levels of the devices that drivers built into the kernel might be bound to are passed on the kernel command line instead, see below.

For devices on the buses listed in HoldProbing= in device-accept.conf5, the kernel does not probe drivers on its own while the service runs, which avoids both problems for devices that are added later. The service binds drivers to these devices itself, once it has applied the configuration to them.

refsect1.title: Acceptance Flow
refsect1.para: The service decides whether a driver is bound to a device that has none yet and is on one of the buses listed in HoldProbing= in device-accept.conf5. If a file in accept.d5 selects the device, it goes through these steps, in this order:

listitem.para: connect: make an SPDM connection to the device, which authenticates it.
measure: obtain the measurements of the device.
log: write the measurements to a log.
extend: extend the log into the root of trust.
verify: run a local verifier on the measurements.
run: put the device into the TDISP RUN state.
bind: apply the trust level, and bind a driver to the device, unless the trust level could not be applied or is disabled.

refsect1.para: If a step fails, the device is rejected: the remaining steps are skipped, its trust level is set to disabled, and no driver is bound to it. A device that no file selects is bound to a driver right away, as it would be by the kernel. A device that is accepted, but no driver could be bound to, for example because none is loaded yet, waits for one: it is probed again when a driver is registered on its bus, and when a driver has been bound to any other device. On reload, the devices that wait for a driver and the ones that have been rejected go through the steps again, with the new configuration.

Note that the steps before bind are not implemented yet, and are skipped: the kernel does not provide the interfaces for making an SPDM connection to a device, for obtaining its measurements and for changing its TDISP state yet, and the other steps build on these.

refsect1.title: Built-in Drivers
refsect1.para: The kernel probes the drivers that are built into it for the devices that exist at boot before the service is started, so that the service cannot change the trust levels of these devices anymore. Hence their trust levels are passed on the kernel command line, with the option device_trust=BUS:DEVICE=LEVEL,…, where DEVICE is the name of the device on the bus. --kernel-cmdline prints this option. It lists the devices that exist, are selected by the configuration, and that a built-in driver might be bound to: the devices that are bound to one, and the ones whose modalias matches an alias of a built-in module. The devices that the option on the command line of the running kernel lists stay listed if the configuration still selects them, as their trust policy might be the reason that no driver is bound to them. An explicit default is included, since it may override a policy initially chosen by the bus. Note that the length of the kernel command line is limited, to 2048 bytes on many architectures, hence the configuration should select the devices precisely.

When a kernel is installed with kernel-install8, its plugin 55-device-accept.install stages this option for the boot loader entry or the unified kernel image. When the command line is inherited from /proc/cmdline, existing device_trust= options are replaced by the current generated policy. This also removes an old policy when the last matching configuration file is deleted. To retain a manually supplied policy across kernel installations, specify it in /etc/kernel/cmdline or another explicit command-line configuration source. An explicit device_trust= option takes precedence over the generated policy, including one set through Cmdline= in uki.conf or a file it references. The plugin does nothing in a container or a chroot, where the devices are not the ones of the machine the kernel is installed for. Hence the kernel has to be installed again after such devices have been added, or the configuration has been changed, e.g. with kernel-install add-all.

listitem.para: Do not change anything and do not wait for uevents, only print the devices that exist and are selected by the configuration, along with the trust level that would be applied and the file that selects them, and exit. Exits with a non-zero exit status if the trust level cannot be applied to some of these devices, for example because they do not have the attribute. The buses listed in HoldProbing= are logged, but driver probing is not changed for them.

Do not change anything and do not wait for uevents, only print the kernel command line option with the trust levels of the devices that a built-in driver might be bound to, see above, and exit. Nothing is printed if there are none. The modules of the kernel of the specified version, or of the running kernel if none is specified, are read from modules.dep and modules.builtin.modinfo in /usr/lib/modules/VERSION/. If these files do not exist, all the devices that are selected are listed.

Upon reception of the SIGHUP process signal, systemd-device-accept-d reloads the configuration files, turns driver probing off or back on for the buses that were added to or removed from HoldProbing=, and applies the configuration to the devices that exist again. Use systemctl reload systemd-device-accept-d.service to do this, which returns once it is done.
